turns.learner: Hello! I want to practise understanding how a speaker feels from what they say.
turns.tutor:
Hello! Great choice. Let's start with one short dialogue.

A: Can you help me move on Saturday?
B: Well, I suppose so, if I have to.

How does B feel: eager, reluctant or angry? Tell me which words made you choose.

turns.learner: I think B is eager, because he says I suppose so, so he agrees to help.
turns.tutor:
Good, you found the key words. B does agree to help. But look at "I suppose so" and "if I have to". These hedges show B does not really want to help. Compare:

1. "Yes, of course! I'd love to!"
2. "Well, I suppose so, if I have to."

Which one sounds eager? What do you think B feels in number 2?

turns.learner: Number 1 is eager. Number 2 is also a bit eager, but less strong. He says yes politely.
turns.tutor:
Number 1 is eager, yes. But number 2 is not "less eager". It is reluctant. B says yes, but does not want to.

Why? "Well" shows hesitation. "I suppose" means "I am not sure". "If I have to" means "I would rather not".

Try this one: A: Can you work late tonight? B: I suppose I could, if nobody else can. Eager or reluctant?

turns.learner: Oh, so I suppose means not sure. Then he is reluctant, because he says if nobody else can.
turns.tutor:
Exactly! Reluctant. You used his words, "if nobody else can", to decide. Well done.

Now a different feeling. A: The train is cancelled. B: Oh great, that is exactly what I needed.

Is B delighted, annoyed or worried? Which words help you decide?

turns.learner: I think annoyed. The train is cancelled, so it is bad, but he says great, so maybe sarcastic?
turns.tutor:
Yes! B is annoyed, and B is sarcastic. B says "great" but means the opposite. You noticed that the words do not match the situation. Very good.

Last one. A: Can you help me paint my room? B: Well... I suppose I could. Eager or reluctant? Why?

turns.learner: Reluctant, because of the Well and the dots, and I suppose. He is not sure he wants to.
turns.tutor:
Perfect! Reluctant. "Well", the pause (...) and "I suppose" are all hedges. They show B says yes but does not really want to.

Remember: a hesitant yes is not an eager yes. Eager speakers say things like "Sure! I'd love to!" Great work today.
